source.title: Scaling Near-Optimal SFT-RL Annotation Budget Allocation from Small to Large LLMs
source.authors: Jing-Tan Wang; A. Verma; Xiao-Qiang Lin; Zhengyuan Liu; Nancy F. Chen; Daniela Rus; B. Low

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses pretraining scaling laws, but its experiments concern post-training allocation between SFT and RL. They do not test held-out pretraining loss scaling or parameter-token allocation under a fixed pretraining compute budget.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results on cross-scale transfer of SFT–RL annotation allocations, a related but different construct. These are recorded with versions ["none"]. Its mentions of pretraining scaling laws and results from cited work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures how the near-optimal SFT–RL annotation-allocation region varies across model sizes and transfers from small proxies to larger targets during post-training. It reports no pretraining loss, no power-law fits in parameters, tokens or compute, no parameter–token compute-optimal split, and no architecture-shape comparison. Its downstream metrics serve as inputs to allocation-region estimates; no scaling curve of downstream performance is fitted or tested. Pretraining scaling laws are cited only as background and as a precedent for excluding pre-convergence points.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the near-optimal SFT–RL allocation region is wide even at 2–10% tolerance, widens with model scale, and transfers reliably from small proxies to larger targets. They report this across tasks, families, DPO and GRPO, and cost asymmetry. They also note that the widening may be partly driven by peak-performance scaling. They frame the result as an empirical recipe, not a universal scaling law, given that post-training scaling is fragile.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies SFT–RL post-training annotation-budget allocation, not the original studies' pretraining loss measurements or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Allocation-region width and transfer vary with task, model family, training method, budget regime, tolerance definition, and annotation-cost ratio. The paper also reports stronger fluctuations for GRPO, especially on Helpfulness.

fits_no_version.finding: Near-optimal SFT–DPO/GRPO allocation regions generally widen with model size at fixed relative tolerance. The widening is partly a relative-tolerance artifact: under an absolute tolerance, Llama-Math shows a negative slope (App. E.6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-training SFT–RL allocation flexibility grows with model scale and transfers from small proxies to larger targets.

fits_no_version.finding: A small-proxy sweep selects a ratio within the target model's near-optimal region in 94.3% (ε=5%) and 97.1% (ε=10%) of cases. It beats or matches a fixed r=0.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Near-optimal SFT–RL annotation allocations transfer from small proxy models to larger targets in the tested settings.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Main experiments use single-seed point estimates; three-seed validation covers only Llama math and summarization. Experiments use LoRA, a five-point allocation grid for the main sweep, task-specific in-distribution data, and model scales up to 14B. The paper states that results may not extend to out-of-distribution evaluation or untested RL algorithms.
record.rows_left_out: No results on pretraining loss scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation were reported. Other qualitative allocation-width and cost-asymmetry results are summarized in r1–r4 rather than split into every task, family, and figure condition.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolating fitted power laws to predict the loss of larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token counts under a pretraining compute budget.
Depth, width or other shape effects on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other modalities, or in fine-tuning or transfer regimes. No power law is fitted to fine-tuning performance.
Downstream performance as a predictable function of scale or pretraining loss. Performance-versus-budget curves are shown but not fitted or tested for predictability.
Dependence of exponents or the compute-optimal split on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Off-topic for pretraining scaling laws. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as background and as a precedent for excluding pre-convergence points. The GPU-time budget case study (Tables 7–8) concerns SFT/DPO cost ratios, not V3. Row r12's state should be corrected to 'absent' because proxy and fixed-ratio reliability are tied.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Predicting larger-run pretraining loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
The compute-optimal parameter and token counts under fixed pretraining compute; the paper instead studies SFT–RL allocation under annotation budgets.
Effects of architecture details such as depth and width on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes as specified in the claim.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of pretraining scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, and Qwen 3 model families (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared near-optimal SFT–DPO allocation-region width across model sizes.
rows.measure: Near-optimal allocation-region width versus model size
rows.value: Generally widens with model scale across tasks and families; the paper notes local non-monotonicity.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative statement about post-training allocation regions, not a pretraining loss scaling result.

rows.subject: Qwen 2.5 model family
rows.size_stated: multiple scales; up to 14B in the additional-scale analysis
rows.operation_detail: Compared near-optimal allocation-region width across model sizes.
rows.measure: Near-optimal allocation-region width versus model size
rows.value: The region narrows marginally at larger scales.
rows.note: The authors attribute this to a possible saturation effect; cross-scale transfer remains strong.

rows.subject: Llama 3 model family
rows.operation_detail: Compared near-optimal allocation-region width and cross-scale transfer.
rows.measure: Near-optimal region widening and transfer across model scales
rows.value: The qualitative pattern matches SFT–DPO: regions widen with tolerance and near-optimal regions transfer more reliably than the point optimum; fluctuations are somewhat stronger, particularly on Helpfulness.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative report for the tested tasks.

rows.subject: Llama model family
rows.operation_detail: Compared near-optimal allocation regions and their transfer under heterogeneous annotation costs.
rows.measure: Near-optimal region width and cross-scale transfer
rows.value: Larger tolerances produce broader regions and stronger transfer; the region generally widens as ρ increases.
rows.note: The budget is monetary annotation cost, not pretraining compute.
